figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Action efficiency across 25 public ARC-AGI-3 environments. Sarbloh (open-weight Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on one GPU) leads five frontier API baselines on 21 of 25 games (72.5% peak mean vs. 59.4% single-pass mean; 100% on 13 games). Because the strict 9-hour Kaggle ceiling precludes exhausting all 25 games in one pass, the curve reports the best score per game across runs, including isolated re-evaluations on complex environments (bp35).
figures.headline: Sarbloh leads five frontier API baselines on 21 of 25 public games, and resolves 13 games fully.
citing_sentences: On public environments, Sarbloh achieves an aggregate mean score of 72.5 across evaluation trials, outperforming proprietary frontier models evaluated via unconstrained APIs on 21 of 25 games and achieving 100% resolution on 13 games (Figure 1).

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Controlled ablation of input observation modalities. Action expenditure required to resolve the opening level of ls20 across four representation tiers using an identical frontier reasoning model (Gemini 3.1 Pro, greedy decoding, single exploratory trial $n=1$ on 12 October 2026). Serializing the environment as raw integer tokens causes budget exhaustion, whereas rendered visual rasters and programmatic geometric relations achieve super-human efficiency ($6$ actions versus human baseline $\approx$10).
figures.headline: Raw integer grids exhaust the ls20 action budget, while code-based search clears the level in 6 actions.
citing_sentences: We evaluated an identical frontier reasoning model (Gemini 3.1 Pro via commercial API, greedy decoding at temperature $T=0$, evaluated in a single diagnostic trial $n=1$ on 12 October 2026) on the opening level of the official environment ls20, holding the prompt template and environment state transitions strictly invariant while altering only the input observation representation (Figure 2).

It draws structure (floor in light tones, walls hatched, the lattice as fine lines, look-alike shapes joined by dashed threads, tethers marked with rings and the HUD magnified in a side panel (Figure 5d)).

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Share of each request’s prompt tokens served from the prefix cache (moving mean over 25 requests), for the first 960 requests of two Qwen3.8-Flash-Next runs on SGLang. Before (15 games): the picture is sent as an unstored last message and the GPU slot changes hands every turn, so each request rewrites the end of the one before. After (Run A, 25 games): every request is the previous request plus its reply, and a game keeps its slot for 20 requests. Labels on the right give the whole run.
figures.headline: Append-only requests raise prefix-cache share over the first 960 requests compared with the earlier design.
citing_sentences: Across our full benchmark run, 98.4% of 1.78 B prompt tokens were served directly from cache, reducing prefill to 1.3% of busy time and rendering execution decode-bound (Figure 6).

figures.caption: Perception Lab rubric score versus token cost. The Fused Briefing establishes an empirical Pareto frontier, scoring 25/28 against 3/28 for the Legacy Encoder while reducing prompt tokens by nearly an order of magnitude.
figures.headline: Fused Briefing sits on the Pareto frontier, scoring 25 of 28 against 3 for the Legacy Encoder at far fewer prompt tokens.
citing_sentences: As detailed in Table 3 and Figure 7, our initial baseline (the Legacy Encoder, arc_eye) scored only 3 of 28 points despite consuming 3,500 text tokens per frame.
The results are in Section 5.1 (Table 3, Figure 7 and Table 4).

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: Action efficiency and score error budget. (a) Distribution of agent-to-human action ratios ($a_{l}/h_{l}$) across 143 cleared levels (Run A, briefing off), where hatched bars indicate performance surpassing human baselines. (b) Decomposition of the 40.6 total points lost from a perfect score, illustrating that 72% of lost credit stems from uncleared levels stalled by perceptual misinduction rather than action overhead on resolved levels.
figures.headline: Uncleared levels stalled by perceptual misinduction account for 72% of the 40.6 points lost.
citing_sentences: In Run A (briefing off: the briefing and map were disabled, so the run characterizes the action interface, serving loop, and scheduler), the agent cleared 143 of 183 levels across the 25 public games in 8.2 hours, recording a median action ratio of 0.77 and a single-pass mean score of 59.4%, with 66% of cleared levels matching or outperforming the human baseline (Figure 8a).
This run provides the baseline for our score decomposition (Figure 8b, 40.6 total points lost from a perfect 100).
We decomposed the 40.6 total points lost from a perfect benchmark score using official RHAE weighting (Figure 8b).

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: Evaluation trajectory across completed submissions on the official held-out Kaggle benchmark. Submissions are ordered by intervention, not by date: each sits in the stage of the last intervention it carried, and every stage has the same width. The solid curve tracks the best score so far, hollow markers indicate regressions and failed experiments, and each label gives the stage’s best score and its gain over the stages before it. The last stage’s submission also changed the level memory and the context drain (Section 5.3). The official hidden-set score (16.53, produced with the full perception engine active) is evaluated on the competition-wide RHAE metric across undisclosed games, whereas Figure 1 reports per-game action efficiency percentages on public environments.
figures.headline: Official hidden-set score climbs with each intervention, peaking at 16.53 after perception engine integration.
citing_sentences: Because the official Kaggle benchmark executes offline on undisclosed environments, it provides an uncontaminated measure of out-of-distribution reasoning (Figure 9).

Crucially, this is Run A, which ran with the briefing and map disabled and characterizes the action interface, serving loop, and scheduler (Appendix C.4); in contrast, the official hidden-set score of 16.53 was produced with the full perception engine active (Figure 9).

figures.headline: Sarbloh clears levels faster than the first Milestone winner, reaching 143 of 183 levels in 8.2 hours.
citing_sentences: As shown in Figure 10, Sarbloh consistently accelerated discovery, clearing 73 levels versus 54 at one hour, 97 versus 63 at two hours, and finishing at 143 of 183 levels in 8.2 hours versus 129 distinct levels for the baseline.

figures.caption: System topology of Sarbloh. The host-side perception engine extracts invariant relations and affordance hypotheses from each frame, passing views to an append-only context. The reasoning model generates Python search routines in a persistent kernel, committing multi-step paths via await play(). Twenty-five games share ten GPU execution slots under the utility-driven priority scheduler.
figures.headline: Perception output feeds an append-only context, and twenty-five games share ten GPU slots under a scheduler.
citing_sentences: Figure 11 shows the whole system.

abstract: Sample-efficient fluid intelligence requires autonomous agents that rapidly form operational models of unfamiliar interactive environments. ARC-AGI-3 evaluates this ability across uninstructed visual games under Relative Human Action Efficiency, penalizing exploratory waste quadratically. When frontier reasoning models interact with raw integer grids, discrete serialization destroys spatial topology, inducing perceptual misinduction where models squander hundreds of actions rediscovering elementary boundaries and symmetries. We introduce Sarbloh, an autonomous open-weight agent architecture structured on the premise that spatial perception, rather than planning capacity, governs interactive reasoning on ARC-AGI-3. A zero-parameter, $\mathcal{O}(HW)$ perception engine reconstructs frames in 35 ms into an object inventory with bipartite temporal tracking, a geometric briefing separating proven invariants from affordance hypotheses under the Measured–Guessed Rule, and an annotated spatial canvas. Paired with a speculative code-as-action runtime, the agent synthesizes algorithmic hypotheses rather than low-level motor primitives. Across eight structural presentations, grounded perception elevates benchmark rubric acquisition from $3/28$ to $25/28$ points ($8.3\times$) while reducing token consumption by $89.4\%$. On twenty-three held-out games, geometric invariants generalize unconditionally with $100\%$ spatial accuracy, whereas single-frame affordance guesses drop to between $6\%$ and $50\%$, confirming the necessity of active hypothesis verification probes. In public evaluation, Run A (briefing off; it characterizes the action interface, serving loop, and scheduler) resolved 143 of 183 levels in 8.2 hours with a median human action ratio of $0.77\times$ and $59.4\%$ single-pass efficiency, with error decompositions attributing seventy-two percent of unearned score loss to perceptual misinduction on stalled environments; Run B (briefing on) recorded $0.68\times$ and $63.5\%$ single-pass efficiency. Within the official nine-hour budget on a single Kaggle NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU, Sarbloh evaluated on the held-out benchmark with the full perception engine active, achieving an official hidden Kaggle score of 16.53, advancing $13.7\times$ beyond the first Milestone winner.

sections.body: ARC-AGI-3 tests whether an agent can build a working model of an unfamiliar game. It is scored with Relative Human Action Efficiency (RHAE), which penalizes exploratory actions quadratically. The authors report a preliminary test in which a frontier model spent over 200–300 exploratory actions on an elementary maze given as raw tokens. The same model needed 6–12 actions when given an aligned rendering and geometric breakdown. They name two insights: Perceptual Misinduction, where serialized grids induce flawed spatial models, and the Measured–Guessed Rule, which treats computed geometry as fact and object roles as guesses to test. They present Sarbloh, an open-weight agent with a deterministic perception engine and code-based actions.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Raw integer grids make frontier models waste actions, and Sarbloh addresses this with grounded perception and code actions.

sections.body: Each step gives the agent a grid of at most 64 by 64 cells, with 16 colour indices, and a status showing whether the game is unfinished, won or over. Actions are numbered 1 to 7 plus a reset, and one action takes a screen coordinate. The per-level score is capped at 1.15 and falls with the square of the ratio of agent actions to human actions, so twice the human count keeps 25% of credit. The offline track runs for nine hours on a single Kaggle GPU with no network access, and all weights must be open. Table 1 lists the official hidden-set score of 16.53 for Sarbloh and 1.21 for the first Milestone winner. Frontier systems run under unbounded conditions.
sections.heading: Preliminaries
sections.headline: ARC-AGI-3 gives colour grids and scores each level by action count, penalizing extra actions quadratically.

sections.body: A single-trial diagnostic ran Gemini 3.1 Pro with greedy decoding on the opening level of ls20, changing only the input format. A raw 64×64 integer matrix led to 200 to 300 actions and budget exhaustion. A rendered raster of the same board needed 12 to 24 actions, a structural decomposition needed 12, and Python search needed 6. The human baseline is approximately 10. Over 90% of the efficiency gain came from structuring perception rather than from longer reasoning. With an oracle briefing on a harder level, the model cleared it in 6 actions. Without the briefing, the agent spent its full budget on inert visual artifacts. The authors state that one trial has limited statistical variance and was used only to isolate the failure.
sections.heading: Motivation: Perception as the Primary Bottleneck
sections.headline: Perception, not planning, limited a frontier model: raw grids cost 200 to 300 actions, code search cleared the level in 6.

sections.body: This section formalizes the Measured–Guessed Rule. Properties computed exactly from the grid, such as reachability, enclosure, midpoint tethers and dihedral symmetry, are stated as fact. Object roles are stated as guesses, each with a one-action test. A host-side engine builds three views per frame that share object identifiers, tracked by a five-pass bipartite matching. Role scores cover eight roles, and each top guess is printed with its confidence and its test. The briefing took a median of 42 ms and the picture 40 ms. The runtime keeps an append-only context so the prefix cache is reused, and a context drain cuts history from 118k to 55k tokens. The authors note that role guesses were right about half the time or less on held-out games.
sections.heading: Methodology
sections.headline: Facts are computed exactly from the grid, while object roles are labeled as guesses with a test.

sections.body: A perception lab compared nine presentations of ls20 and r11l on a pre-registered 28-point rubric. The Legacy Encoder scored 3 of 28 at 3,500 text tokens per frame. The Fused Briefing scored 25 of 28 at 370 tokens, an 89.4% reduction. On 23 held-out games, grid reconstruction was exact in 23/23 games. Single-frame guesses generalized poorly. Agent identity was right in 6/14 keyboard games, the moves-left gauge in 10/20, click handles in 7/29, and forward foresight in 1/16 games. The rubric was graded against an answer key without blinding. On public games, Run A cleared 143 of 183 levels in 8.2 hours, with a median action ratio of 0.77 and a single-pass mean of 59.4.
sections.heading: Results
sections.headline: Perception lifts the rubric from 3 to 25 of 28, and the official hidden score reaches 16.53.

sections.body: Earlier interactive agents pass the grid to the model as raw data. The first Milestone winner, the Duck harness, serializes the board as text character matrices alongside rendered frames. The second and third Kaggle systems pass annotated screenshots to Gemma-4-31B, which emits action sequences. Arcgentica and Prime Agent give the model a persistent Python session over raw coordinate arrays. Sarbloh instead computes lattice reachability, enclosures and symmetries on the host in time linear in grid size, and tracks entities across steps. It builds on CodeAct, which found executable code actions outperform structured action schemas. It combines code simulation and action in one `await play()` call.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Earlier interactive agents pass raw grids to the model, while Sarbloh computes geometric invariants on the host.

sections.body: The authors list three limits. First, the perception engine evaluates affordance hypotheses independently at each frame and keeps no unified belief distribution over multi-step episodes. Second, once a level is understood the agent plans efficiently, but failures on complex perceptual transitions remain the main source of score loss. Third, results rely on general-purpose open-weight models with no task-specific fine-tuning. Future work proposes belief updating from falsification probes, parameter-efficient fine-tuning on verified trajectories, and offline reinforcement learning with Group Relative Policy Optimization. The paper does not test any of these.
sections.heading: Limitations and Future Work
sections.headline: Limits: hypotheses are checked frame by frame without a unified belief, and no task-specific fine-tuning is used.

sections.body: The authors conclude that interactive reasoning is limited by perception more than by planning. They argue that unparsed coordinate matrices induce misinduction that wastes actions. They propose the Measured–Guessed Rule, which computes invariants on the host and tests guesses with one-action probes, as the remedy. They state that advancing fluid intelligence on unseen benchmarks does not strictly require larger parameter scales or unconstrained inference budgets. The evidence offered is the open-weight results in the preceding sections, which come from one benchmark and a single offline GPU configuration.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Perception, not planning, is argued to limit interactive reasoning, so structured perception can keep open-weight models efficient.

sections.body: The appendix gives a notation table and the priority scheduler, with its hope factor and weights. It lists hyperparameters for Runs A and B and the perception lab protocol, with its answer key and full briefings for ls20 and r11l. It also covers four more games for the perception pipeline, and edge cases such as lattice collapse and relation crowding. Runtime failure modes include a degenerate holding loop that used 1.24 B of the run's 1.78 B prompt tokens. A telemetry table and a two-run comparison are included. The code is released under a public-domain-equivalent licence, with scripts that produce the figures.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists notation, the scheduler, hyperparameters, lab protocols, failure modes, telemetry, and reproducible artifacts.
